**Machine Six**

The dryers at the Sunbeam sound like a train that never arrives. That's what I thought my first night, back when I still had the energy for metaphors. Now I mostly think in quarters. Quarters for the wash, quarters for the dry, quarters for the candy machine that takes your money and gives you nothing, which is its own kind of honesty.

I work eleven to seven, five nights a week. Three years now. People think a laundromat at 3 a.m. would be empty, but the city at that hour is a different country, and its citizens are insomniacs, nurses, cabdrivers, and people who have run out of other places to be. One fluorescent tube buzzes like it's clearing its throat to speak, then deciding against it. There's a bulletin board with a flyer for a missing cat named Duchess, dated 2019. The cat is definitely gone. The flyer stays. At the Sunbeam we understand about waiting.

The regulars come in a rotation, like weather. Tuesdays it's Priya, who works labor and delivery and sometimes sits with her eyes closed while her scrubs go around, still carrying that hospital smell, which is clean and terrible at once. She never sleeps in the chair. She says if she sleeps she'll miss the spin cycle, and the spin cycle is the closest thing she gets to a conclusion. Thursdays, two brothers bring garbage bags of clothes from their mother's house — she moved to assisted living in October — and they fight quietly about which of them their mother likes less. It's closer than you'd think. Fridays a kid named Marcus washes his basketball uniform at midnight over a superstition involving free throws, and I have learned not to argue with a man and his free throws.

And then there's the old man.

He comes in around two, Sundays, when the place is at its emptiest. He is tall the way old tall men are, stooped like a question mark that has given up on the answer. He uses machine six, the one by the window, and he washes a single pillowcase. White cotton, gone soft gray at the fold. No other clothes. He sits with his hands on his knees for the forty minutes the machine runs, watching it like television. Then he takes the pillowcase out, folds it into a neat square, puts it inside his coat, and leaves. He has never once used a dryer. Whatever he is drying, he dries it at home, or he dries it nowhere.

I have had three years to ask him about it. I never have. There's a rule I made without deciding to: you don't ask the night people why. Night is where people bring the things that can't sit in the daylight laundromat of their lives, the things that would look like nothing in the morning — a pillowcase, a bag of a dead mother's blouses, a uniform that has to be washed at midnight or the free throws will know. You don't go pawing through that. The machines do the washing. That's already more intimacy than most of us can stand.

Last winter I learned his name by accident. The dry cleaner next door, Mrs. Bao, was shoveling the sidewalk, and he stopped to take the shovel from her and finish the job, and she called him Mr. Ander. Just that. Mr. Ander, thank you, Mr. Ander, go inside before you fall. He nodded at me like we were strangers, which technically we were, and which by then we were not.

In February I tore my meniscus on the ice outside and sat in the office with it raised on a milk crate, and I heard machine six start without looking. When I came out to change the bathroom sign, he was sitting forward, and the pillowcase — I couldn't help seeing — had a tear in it, a long one, like it had given up a seam. He held the folded square in his lap when the cycle ended, and he sat with it a while, the way you sit with a decision.

The next Sunday the tear was mended. Badly. Someone had sewn it up with thread that didn't match, big blobs of stitches, the kind of sewing that is really just apologizing to a thing for not letting it go. My grandmother mended everything twice, once for strength and once for looks, and she said the second mending was for God. Mr. Ander's mending was the first kind only.

In March he brought a second pillowcase. Same white cotton, same gray fold, but a different case — I could tell because the first one had a small brown stain near the seam that I had stopped pretending not to notice. He washed them both. He sat with his hands on his knees. He folded them both into squares, put them both inside his coat, and left, and I understood that something had happened, though I couldn't have said what. A drawer emptied, maybe. A decision about a bed. The second pillowcase arriving the way a second truth arrives: quietly, after the first one has been carried alone for years.

He stopped coming in April.

I want to tell you I asked Mrs. Bao, that I found an obituary, that I learned the whole story — the wife, the bed, the years. I didn't. I want to tell you I kept his pillowcase, that it's in a drawer. It isn't. What I have is machine six, which I still run empty some Sunday nights around two, when the place is at its emptiest — a quarter in the slot, forty minutes of water going around for no one. The other attendants think I'm testing it. Let them.

The dryers still sound like a train that never arrives. I know now that the point of a train sound is not the arriving. It's that while it sounds, you are somewhere, and something of yours is turning, getting cleaner, getting ready to be folded into a square and carried home.

**Night Wash**

The dryers at the Sunbeam sound like a train that never arrives. That's what I thought my first night, back when I still had the energy for metaphors. Now I mostly think in quarters. Quarters for the wash, quarters for the dry, quarters for the candy machine that takes your money and gives you nothing, which is its own kind of honesty.

I work eleven to seven, five nights a week. Three years now. People think a laundromat at 3 a.m. would be empty, but the city at that hour is a different country, and its citizens are insomniacs, nurses, cabdrivers, and people who have run out of other places to be. The fluorescent light never fully flickers off; one tube over the folding table buzzes like it's clearing its throat to say something and then deciding against it. There's a bulletin board with a flyer for a missing cat named Duchess, dated 2019. The cat is definitely gone. The flyer stays. Nobody takes it down. At the Sunbeam we understand about waiting.

The regulars come in a kind of rotation, like weather. Tuesdays it's Priya, who works labor and delivery and sometimes sits in the plastic chair with her eyes closed while her scrubs go around, still smelling faintly of that hospital smell, which is clean and terrible at once. She never sleeps in the chair. She says if she sleeps she'll miss the spin cycle, and the spin cycle is the closest thing she gets to a conclusion. Thursdays, two brothers come in with garbage bags of clothes from their mother's house — she moved to assisted living in October — and they fight quietly about which of them their mother likes less. It's closer than you'd think. Fridays a kid named Marcus washes his basketball uniform at midnight because of some superstition involving free throws, and I have learned not to argue with a man and his free throws.

And then there's the old man.

He comes in around two, Sundays, when the place is at its emptiest. He is tall the way old tall men are, stooped like a question mark that has given up on the answer. He uses machine six, the one by the window, and he washes a single pillowcase. White cotton, gone soft gray at the fold. No other clothes. He sits with his hands on his knees for the forty minutes the machine runs, watching it like it's television. Then he takes the pillowcase out, folds it into a neat square, puts it inside his coat, and leaves. He has never once used a dryer. Whatever he is drying, he dries it at home, or he dries it nowhere.

I have had three years to ask him about it. I never have. There is a rule I made without deciding to: you don't ask the night people why. The night is where people bring the things that can't sit in the daylight laundromat of their lives, the things that would look like nothing in the morning — a pillowcase, a bag of a dead mother's blouses, a uniform that has to be washed at midnight or the free throws will know. You don't go pawing through that. The machines do the washing. That's already more intimacy than most of us can stand.

Last winter I found out his name by accident. The dry cleaner next door, Mrs. Bao, was shoveling the sidewalk, and he stopped to take the shovel from her and finish the job, and she called him Mr. Ander. Just that. Mr. Ander, thank you, Mr. Ander, go inside before you fall. He nodded at me like we were strangers, which technically we were, and which by then we were not.

In February I tore the meniscus in my knee slipping on the ice outside, and I sat in the office with it raised on a milk crate, and I heard machine six start without me having to look. When I came out to change the sign on the bathroom, he was sitting forward, and the pillowcase — I couldn't help seeing — had a tear in it, a long one, like it had given up a seam. He was holding the folded square in his lap when the cycle ended, and he sat with it a while, the way you sit with a decision.

The next Sunday the tear was mended. Badly. Someone had sewn it up with a thread that didn't match, biglops of stitches, the kind of sewing that is really just apologizing to a thing for not letting it go. I thought about my grandmother, who mended everything twice, once for strength and once for looks, and who said the second mending was for God. Mr. Ander's mending was the first kind only.

In March he brought a second pillowcase. Same white cotton, same gray fold, but a different case — I could tell because the first one had a small brown stain near the seam that I had long ago stopped pretending not to notice. He washed them both. He sat with his hands on his knees. He folded them both into squares and put them both inside his coat and left, and I understood that something had happened, though I couldn't have said what. A drawer emptied, maybe. A decision about a bed. The second pillowcase arriving in the world the way a second truth arrives: quietly, after the first one has been carried alone for years.

He stopped coming in April.

I want to tell you I asked Mrs. Bao, that I found an obituary, that I learned the whole story — the wife, the bed, the eleven years. I didn't. I want to tell you I kept his pillowcase, that I have it in a drawer. I don't. What I have is machine six, which I still run empty sometimes on Sunday nights around two, when the place is at its emptiest, a quarter in the slot, forty minutes of water going around for no one. The other attendants think I'm testing it. Let them.

The dryers still sound like a train that never arrives. I know now that the point of a train sound is not the arriving. It's that while it sounds, you are somewhere, and something of yours is turning, getting cleaner, getting ready to be folded into a square and carried home.
